description: Core Kubernetes from architecture to security, plus the surrounding cloud-native stack (Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, Istio, Cilium, LFCS Linux). Organised by concept for a platform/enterprise architect working in production and preparing for the CKA, CKAD, CKS, KCNA and KCSA (Kubestronaut) exams.

notes.front: What core problem does Kubernetes solve?
notes.back: It's a container orchestrator: you declare desired state and it schedules, runs, heals and scales containers across a cluster of nodes, instead of you managing individual machines.
notes.analogy: Like an air-traffic control tower: aircraft (containers) don't pick their own runways; the tower assigns slots and reroutes them when a runway closes.

notes.text: A Kubernetes cluster has {{c1::control plane}} nodes, which manage the cluster, and {{c2::worker}} nodes, which run the application pods.

Kubernetes control plane components: {{c1::kube-apiserver}} (the front end everything talks to), {{c2::kube-scheduler}} (assigns pods to nodes), {{c3::kube-controller-manager}} (runs the reconciliation loops), {{c4::etcd}} (key-value store of all cluster state).
Components on every Kubernetes worker node: the {{c1::kubelet}} (node agent that runs pods), {{c2::kube-proxy}} (programs Service routing), and the {{c3::container runtime}} (e.g. containerd, CRI-O).

notes.front: In Kubernetes, what is etcd's role, and which component talks to it directly?
notes.back: The consistent (Raft-based) key-value store holding all cluster state, the single source of truth. Only the API server reads and writes it.

notes.front: Why is the API server called the hub of the Kubernetes architecture?
notes.back: It validates and persists every object to etcd and is the only component touching etcd. All other components watch it and never talk to each other directly.
notes.analogy: A hub-and-spoke airline network: every flight goes through the hub; there are no direct flights between spokes.

notes.front: What does kube-scheduler do, and what does it not do?
notes.back: Watches for pods with no node assigned, filters feasible nodes, scores them, and writes the binding. It doesn't start the pod; the kubelet does.

notes.front: What is kube-controller-manager?
notes.back: One process running many built-in controllers (ReplicaSet, Deployment, Node, EndpointSlice…), each a loop driving actual state toward desired state.

notes.front: What is the kubelet's job?
notes.back: The node agent: watches for pods bound to its node, has the container runtime (via CRI) run them, runs their probes, and reports pod and node status to the API server.

notes.front: What is the Kubernetes reconciliation (control) loop?
notes.back: Each controller continuously compares desired state (spec) with observed state (status) and acts to close the gap. It keeps running after deploy time, so drift gets corrected.
notes.analogy: A thermostat: you set the target temperature; it keeps measuring and switching the heater until the room matches, and starts again if someone opens a window.

notes.front: How do Kubernetes components find out that objects changed?
notes.back: They open a watch on the API server and receive change events instead of polling, which is cheap and near real-time.

notes.front: Imperative vs declarative management in Kubernetes?
notes.back: Imperative: commands that say how (kubectl create, scale). Declarative: you submit the desired end state (manifests, kubectl apply) and controllers reconcile toward it.
notes.analogy: Imperative is giving a taxi driver turn-by-turn directions; declarative is just giving the address.

notes.front: Which Kubernetes component does kubectl actually talk to?
notes.back: Only the API server (REST over HTTPS, with credentials from kubeconfig). It never contacts nodes or etcd directly.

notes.front: What do Kubernetes namespaces provide, and what do they not provide?
notes.back: A scope for names, RBAC, quotas and policies (soft multi-tenancy). They do not isolate network traffic; that needs NetworkPolicies.

notes.text: Kubernetes plugs in implementations through standard interfaces: {{c1::CRI}} for container runtimes, {{c2::CNI}} for pod networking, {{c3::CSI}} for storage drivers.
notes.analogy: Like USB ports: the laptop defines the socket, and any vendor's device that fits the standard works.
notes.extra: Why: the core stays vendor-neutral; runtimes, networks and storage can be swapped without changing Kubernetes.

notes.front: Under the kubelet, what do containerd/CRI-O do vs runc?
notes.back: containerd / CRI-O: CRI runtimes that pull images and manage container lifecycles. runc: the low-level OCI runtime that actually creates the container process.
notes.extra: History that matters: dockershim was removed (1.24), so the kubelet no longer drives Docker directly; Docker-built images still run fine (they're OCI images).

notes.front: What is a CustomResourceDefinition (CRD)?
notes.back: It registers a new resource type with the API server, so custom objects (e.g. kind: Database) are stored in etcd and managed with kubectl like built-ins.

notes.front: What is the Operator pattern?
notes.back: A custom controller plus CRDs that encodes an application's operational knowledge (provisioning, backups, upgrades, failover) and reconciles it continuously, turning runbooks into automation.
notes.analogy: A robot SRE that knows only one database, but knows it deeply and never sleeps.
notes.extra: Depth: controller implementation patterns live in the Platform Engineering / Go decks.

notes.front: What is a Pod?
notes.back: The smallest deployable unit: one or more containers that are always co-scheduled on one node and share a network namespace (one IP, one port space) and, optionally, volumes.
notes.analogy: Containers in a pod are roommates: same street address and shared kitchen (volumes), separate bedrooms (filesystems/processes).

notes.front: When should two containers share a Pod rather than run in separate Pods?
notes.back: Only when tightly coupled and needing shared network/files, e.g. an app plus its sidecar. Independent components go in separate pods so they scale and fail independently.

notes.text: Multi-container pod patterns: a {{c1::sidecar}} assists the main container (e.g. log shipper), an {{c2::ambassador}} proxies its connections to the outside world, an {{c3::adapter}} normalizes its output for consumers.

notes.front: How is a native sidecar container declared (Kubernetes 1.29+)?
notes.back: As an initContainer with restartPolicy: Always: it starts before the app containers, keeps running alongside them, and is stopped after them.

notes.front: What is an init container, and when do you use one?
notes.back: A container that runs to completion, in order, before app containers start. Used for setup: wait for a dependency, fetch config, run a migration.

notes.front: What is the pause (infrastructure) container in a Pod?
notes.back: A tiny container that holds the pod's network (and IPC) namespace. App containers join it, so the pod keeps one IP even as app containers restart.

notes.front: What are labels and label selectors for?
notes.back: Labels are key-value pairs on objects; selectors pick sets of objects by them. This is how Services, ReplicaSets and NetworkPolicies find their pods.

notes.front: Labels vs annotations in Kubernetes?
notes.back: Labels identify and select objects (short, indexed, used by selectors). Annotations hold non-identifying metadata for tools (build info, config hints) and can't be selected on.

notes.front: ReplicaSet vs ReplicationController?
notes.back: Both keep N pod replicas running. ReplicaSet (the successor) adds set-based selectors (in, notin, exists). You rarely create either directly; Deployments manage ReplicaSets.

notes.front: What does a Deployment add over a bare ReplicaSet?
notes.back: Declarative rolling updates and rollback: it creates a new ReplicaSet per revision and shifts pods from the old ReplicaSet to the new one.

notes.front: RollingUpdate vs Recreate Deployment strategy?
notes.back: RollingUpdate (default): replace pods gradually, no downtime, two versions coexist briefly. Recreate: kill all, then start new; downtime, but two versions never run at once.
notes.extra: Not built in: canary and blue-green need extra tooling (Argo Rollouts, a service mesh).

notes.text: In a Deployment RollingUpdate, {{c1::maxSurge}} caps how many pods may exist above the desired count, and {{c2::maxUnavailable}} caps how many may be unavailable during the update.
notes.extra: Both default to 25%. maxUnavailable: 0 + maxSurge: 1 = add-before-remove, safest for capacity.

notes.front: How do you roll back a Deployment, and why is it possible?
notes.back: kubectl rollout undo deploy/<name> [--to-revision=N]. Old ReplicaSets are kept (up to revisionHistoryLimit) and simply scaled back up.

notes.front: DaemonSet vs Deployment: how are pods placed?
notes.back: DaemonSet: exactly one pod per (matching) node, added automatically to new nodes; for node agents (CNI, log/metrics collectors). Deployment: N replicas placed anywhere by the scheduler.

notes.front: Job vs CronJob?
notes.back: Job: runs pods to completion for a finite task (not restarted after success). CronJob: creates Jobs on a cron schedule.

notes.text: In a Job spec, {{c1::completions}} sets how many pods must succeed, {{c2::parallelism}} how many run at once, and {{c3::backoffLimit}} how many retries before the Job is marked failed.

notes.front: What does a StatefulSet guarantee that a Deployment doesn't?
notes.back: Stable per-pod identity: ordinal names (web-0, web-1), stable DNS via a headless Service, per-pod persistent storage, and ordered creation/deletion.
notes.analogy: Deployment pods are interchangeable taxis; StatefulSet pods are numbered seats on a train: each passenger always returns to the same seat and the same luggage rack.

notes.front: Why does a StatefulSet need a headless Service?
notes.back: To give each pod a stable DNS name (web-0.<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local) so peers can reach specific members, which clustered databases and brokers require.

notes.front: How does a StatefulSet give each pod its own persistent storage?
notes.back: volumeClaimTemplates create one PVC per pod (data-web-0, …). A rescheduled pod reattaches to the same PVC, keeping its data.

notes.front: What does the kubelet do when a liveness probe fails?
notes.back: It restarts the container (subject to the pod's restartPolicy).

notes.front: Liveness vs readiness probe: what does each failure do?
notes.back: Liveness fail → container restarted. Readiness fail → pod removed from Service endpoints (no restart) until it passes again.
notes.analogy: Readiness is the 'closed' sign on a shop door; liveness is calling an ambulance for the shopkeeper.

notes.front: What does a startup probe do?
notes.back: It holds off liveness and readiness checks until the app has started, so slow-booting apps aren't killed during startup.

notes.text: Kubernetes probe handlers: {{c1::httpGet}} (2xx/3xx = healthy), {{c2::tcpSocket}} (connection opens), {{c3::exec}} (exit code 0), {{c4::grpc}} (gRPC health check).

notes.front: What goes wrong if a liveness probe checks a downstream dependency such as the database?
notes.back: A DB outage fails every pod's liveness check, so they all restart in a loop: a cascading failure. Liveness should check only the process itself.

notes.front: nodeSelector vs node affinity?
notes.back: Both steer pods to nodes by node labels. nodeSelector is a simple hard equality match. Node affinity adds operators (In, NotIn, Exists) and soft (preferred) rules.

notes.front: How do taints and tolerations work together?
notes.back: A taint on a node repels pods. A matching toleration on a pod allows (but doesn't force) it onto that node.
notes.analogy: A taint is a 'members only' sign on a club door; a toleration is a membership card. Holding a card doesn't make you go to that club.

notes.text: Taint effects: {{c1::NoSchedule}} blocks new pods that don't tolerate it; {{c2::PreferNoSchedule}} avoids the node if possible; {{c3::NoExecute}} also evicts running pods that don't tolerate it.
notes.extra: kubectl taint nodes n1 key=val:NoSchedule; remove with a trailing -.

notes.front: Taints/tolerations vs node affinity: which side does what?
notes.back: Taints let a node repel pods (node-centric); node affinity lets a pod seek nodes (pod-centric). Dedicated nodes usually need both: taint to keep others off, affinity to pull the right pods on.

notes.text: {{c1::Node affinity}} attracts a pod to nodes by node labels; {{c2::pod affinity}} co-locates it with matching pods in the same topology domain; {{c3::pod anti-affinity}} keeps it away from them (e.g. spread replicas across zones).

notes.front: Affinity rules: requiredDuringScheduling… vs preferredDuringScheduling…, and what does IgnoredDuringExecution mean?
notes.back: Required = hard (pod stays Pending if unmet); preferred = weighted soft rule. IgnoredDuringExecution: running pods aren't evicted if labels change later.

notes.front: Container resource request vs limit?
notes.back: Request: the amount the scheduler reserves on a node to place the pod. Limit: the hard runtime cap.

notes.front: What happens when a container exceeds its CPU limit vs its memory limit?
notes.back: CPU: throttled (CPU is compressible). Memory: OOM-killed (memory is incompressible).
notes.analogy: CPU is a tap you can turn down; memory is a glass you can't make smaller, so it overflows.

notes.text: Pod QoS classes: {{c1::Guaranteed}} = every container has requests == limits for CPU and memory; {{c2::Burstable}} = some requests/limits set but not Guaranteed; {{c3::BestEffort}} = none set.

notes.front: Under node memory pressure, in which QoS order are pods evicted?
notes.back: BestEffort first, then Burstable (those furthest over their requests), Guaranteed last.

notes.front: ResourceQuota vs LimitRange?
notes.back: ResourceQuota: aggregate cap for a whole namespace (total CPU/memory, object counts). LimitRange: per-container/pod defaults and min/max, and it auto-fills missing requests/limits.

notes.front: A namespace has a CPU ResourceQuota. What happens to a new pod with no CPU request?
notes.back: It's rejected, unless a LimitRange in the namespace supplies a default request.

notes.front: What does the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) do?
notes.back: Adjusts a workload's replica count to keep a metric (CPU utilization, custom or external metric) near a target.
notes.extra: Pitfall: utilization is a % of the request; no requests set = HPA can't compute CPU utilization. Needs metrics-server.

notes.text: Kubernetes autoscalers: {{c1::HPA}} changes the number of pod replicas; {{c2::VPA}} changes a pod's CPU/memory requests; {{c3::Cluster Autoscaler}} adds/removes nodes when pods are unschedulable or nodes sit idle.

notes.front: What does KEDA add over a plain HPA?
notes.back: Event-driven scaling on external sources (queue length, Kafka lag, cron), including scaling to and from zero.

notes.front: What does the Kubernetes pod network model require?
notes.back: Every pod gets its own IP, and all pods can reach all other pods on any node without NAT; node agents can reach local pods. A CNI plugin implements it.
notes.extra: Pitfall: pod CIDR must not overlap the node or Service CIDRs.

notes.front: What is a Service, and why is it needed?
notes.back: A stable virtual IP + DNS name that load-balances across the pods matching a label selector. Needed because pod IPs change as pods come and go.
notes.analogy: A company switchboard number: it never changes, even as the people (pods) answering behind it come and go.

notes.text: Service types build on each other: {{c1::ClusterIP}} (internal virtual IP, the default) → {{c2::NodePort}} (same port on every node, 30000–32767) → {{c3::LoadBalancer}} (cloud LB in front). {{c4::ExternalName}} is just a DNS CNAME alias.

notes.front: How does external traffic reach a NodePort Service?
notes.back: Clients hit <anyNodeIP>:<nodePort>; the node forwards to a backing pod, which may be on a different node.

notes.front: What does a LoadBalancer Service add, and what's its drawback at scale?
notes.back: The cloud provider provisions an external LB with its own IP that forwards to the node ports. One LB per Service gets expensive, which is why Ingress/Gateway exist.

notes.front: What is a headless Service?
notes.back: A Service with clusterIP: None: no virtual IP; DNS returns the individual ready pod IPs. Used for StatefulSets and client-side discovery.

notes.front: What are Endpoints / EndpointSlices?
notes.back: The list of ready pod IP:port pairs behind a Service, kept in sync by a controller as pods come, go, or change readiness.

notes.front: What does kube-proxy do?
notes.back: On every node it programs the dataplane (iptables or IPVS rules) so traffic to a Service's virtual IP is load-balanced to the backend pods.

notes.front: kube-proxy: iptables mode vs IPVS mode?
notes.back: iptables: rule chains with linear matching; fine for most clusters. IPVS: kernel hash-table load balancer; scales better to thousands of Services and offers more LB algorithms.
notes.extra: eBPF dataplanes (e.g. Cilium) can replace kube-proxy entirely.

notes.front: What provides in-cluster DNS in Kubernetes?
notes.back: CoreDNS, a Deployment behind the kube-dns Service. The kubelet points each pod's /etc/resolv.conf at that Service IP.

notes.text: A Kubernetes Service's DNS name is {{c1::<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local}}.

notes.front: What is an Ingress, and why use it instead of many LoadBalancer Services?
notes.back: An HTTP(S) routing layer (host/path rules) that exposes many Services through one entry point, run by an Ingress controller. Cheaper and more flexible than one cloud LB per Service.
notes.analogy: A hotel receptionist who directs every guest to the right room, instead of giving each room its own street door.

notes.front: Why was the Gateway API created as a successor to Ingress?
notes.back: Ingress is one overloaded object (HTTP only, vendor features via annotations). Gateway API is role-oriented, portable and expressive, covering L4 and L7 (HTTP, gRPC, TCP).

notes.text: Gateway API resources by role: {{c1::GatewayClass}} (the controller/infrastructure type), {{c2::Gateway}} (a listener instance, owned by cluster operators), {{c3::HTTPRoute}} (routing rules, owned by app teams).

notes.front: What does a NetworkPolicy do, and what's needed for it to take effect?
notes.back: An L3/L4 allow-list for ingress/egress of pods selected by labels. It works only if the CNI enforces it (e.g. Calico, Cilium); otherwise it's silently ignored.

notes.front: When does a pod become isolated by NetworkPolicy?
notes.back: Pods are non-isolated by default. Once any policy selects a pod for a direction (ingress or egress), that direction becomes default-deny and only allowed flows pass. Policies are additive.

notes.front: What is a default-deny NetworkPolicy, and why start with it?
notes.back: A policy with podSelector: {} and no allow rules, isolating every pod in the namespace. You then add explicit allows: least-privilege networking.

notes.front: After applying a default-deny egress policy, what usually breaks first?
notes.back: DNS: pods can't reach CoreDNS on port 53 (UDP/TCP) until you explicitly allow it.

notes.front: What is an emptyDir volume?
notes.back: A volume created empty when the pod starts on a node and deleted when the pod is removed. Used for scratch space or sharing files between containers in the pod.

notes.front: What is a hostPath volume, and why avoid it?
notes.back: It mounts a file/directory from the node's filesystem. Data is tied to one node (not portable), and it can expose node files, so it's for node-level system pods only.
notes.extra: Pod Security baseline forbids hostPath volumes.

notes.front: PersistentVolume (PV) vs PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)?
notes.back: PV: a piece of cluster storage (cluster-scoped), provisioned by an admin or dynamically. PVC: a namespaced request for storage (size, access mode) that binds to a matching PV.
notes.analogy: A PVC is a hotel reservation (room size and type); the PV is the actual room the hotel assigns to it.

notes.front: What does a StorageClass enable?
notes.back: Dynamic provisioning: a PVC that names the class makes its provisioner (usually a CSI driver) create a matching PV on demand. No pre-made PVs needed.

notes.front: What problem does volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer solve?
notes.back: It delays provisioning until a pod using the PVC is scheduled, so the volume is created in that pod's zone. Immediate can create it in the wrong zone.

notes.text: PV access modes: {{c1::ReadWriteOnce (RWO)}} = read-write by a single node; {{c2::ReadOnlyMany (ROX)}} = read-only by many nodes; {{c3::ReadWriteMany (RWX)}} = read-write by many nodes; {{c4::ReadWriteOncePod (RWOP)}} = read-write by a single pod.
notes.extra: Pitfall: RWO still lets several pods on the same node mount the volume; use RWOP for true single-writer.

notes.text: PV reclaim policies (after the claim is deleted): {{c1::Retain}} keeps the volume and data for manual cleanup; {{c2::Delete}} removes the backing storage asset; {{c3::Recycle}} (deprecated) scrubbed it for reuse.
notes.extra: Dynamically provisioned PVs inherit the StorageClass reclaimPolicy, default Delete.

notes.front: What is a ConfigMap, and how can a pod consume it?
notes.back: An object holding non-sensitive config as key-value pairs, decoupled from the image. Consumed as environment variables, command args, or files in a mounted volume.

notes.front: How does a Secret differ from a ConfigMap?
notes.back: Same consumption model (env vars or files), but meant for sensitive data: values are base64-encoded, can be mounted on tmpfs, and access can be restricted separately with RBAC.

notes.front: Is a Kubernetes Secret encrypted by default?
notes.back: No. Base64 is encoding, not encryption; Secrets are stored readable in etcd unless encryption at rest is configured.
notes.analogy: Base64 is writing a note in pig Latin: it looks scrambled but anyone can read it.

notes.front: You update a ConfigMap. What happens to pods using it as a volume vs as env vars?
notes.back: Mounted files update automatically after a kubelet sync delay (not with subPath). Env vars never update; the pod must be restarted.

notes.front: What is the Downward API?
notes.back: A way to expose a pod's own metadata (name, namespace, labels, node name, pod IP, resource limits) to its containers as env vars or files, without calling the API server.

notes.text: The 4Cs of cloud native security, outermost to innermost: {{c1::Cloud}} → {{c2::Cluster}} → {{c3::Container}} → {{c4::Code}}.
notes.analogy: Nested Russian dolls: if the outer doll is open, the inner ones are exposed.
notes.extra: A weak outer layer can't be compensated by strong inner layers.

notes.text: Every Kubernetes API request passes {{c1::authentication}} (who are you?) → {{c2::authorization}} (may you do this?) → {{c3::admission control}} (mutate/validate the object) → persistence to etcd.
notes.analogy: Airport: passport check (authn), boarding pass for this flight (authz), then security screening that may tag or confiscate items (admission).

notes.front: How does the API server authenticate users, and what's notably missing?
notes.back: X.509 client certs, bearer tokens (ServiceAccount, OIDC), or an authenticating proxy/webhook. There are no User objects: users exist only as names asserted by credentials.

notes.front: Which Kubernetes authorization modes exist besides RBAC?
notes.back: Node (for kubelets), Webhook (external decision), ABAC (legacy), and AlwaysAllow/AlwaysDeny (testing only).

notes.front: What is a ServiceAccount?
notes.back: An identity for processes in pods (not humans). Each pod runs as one; its token lets the app authenticate to the API server.

notes.front: Why set automountServiceAccountToken: false where a workload doesn't call the API?
notes.back: A mounted token can be stolen from a compromised pod and used against the API server. Don't mount what isn't needed.
notes.extra: Modern tokens are short-lived, audience-bound projected tokens, not long-lived Secrets.

notes.text: RBAC: a {{c1::Role}} grants verbs on resources within one namespace and is granted by a {{c2::RoleBinding}}; a {{c3::ClusterRole}} grants cluster-wide (or reusable) permissions and is granted cluster-wide by a {{c4::ClusterRoleBinding}}.

notes.front: Can Kubernetes RBAC express a deny rule?
notes.back: No. RBAC rules are purely additive allow-lists; anything not granted is denied.

notes.front: Why would you bind a ClusterRole with a namespaced RoleBinding?
notes.back: To reuse one ClusterRole definition (e.g. built-in view, edit) while granting it only inside that RoleBinding's namespace.
notes.extra: A ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding is required for cluster-scoped resources such as nodes and PVs.

notes.front: How do you check whether a subject may perform an action?
notes.back: kubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource> --as <user> -n <ns>, e.g. kubectl auth can-i create deployments --as dev -n web. Add --list for all permissions.
notes.extra: For a ServiceAccount: --as system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<name>.

notes.front: How do you onboard a human user with a client certificate?
notes.back: Submit a CertificateSigningRequest with the base64 CSR, kubectl certificate approve it, put the issued cert in a kubeconfig, then grant RBAC to its CN (user) / O (group).

notes.front: Mutating vs validating admission webhooks?
notes.back: Mutating may modify objects (inject sidecars, set defaults); validating may only accept or reject. Mutating runs first, so validators see the final object.
notes.extra: Policy engines (Kyverno, Gatekeeper) register as these webhooks.

notes.front: What does the ImagePolicyWebhook admission controller do?
notes.back: Sends each pod's image list to an external service that returns allow/deny, enforcing image policy at admission. Configured via --admission-control-config-file, including fail-open vs fail-closed.

notes.front: What replaced PodSecurityPolicy?
notes.back: Pod Security Admission: a built-in admission controller (PSP was removed in 1.25) that enforces the Pod Security Standards per namespace.

notes.text: Pod Security Standards: {{c1::privileged}} = unrestricted; {{c2::baseline}} = blocks known privilege escalations (privileged, hostNetwork, hostPath); {{c3::restricted}} = hardened (non-root, drop ALL caps, seccomp RuntimeDefault).

notes.front: How do you enforce a Pod Security level on a namespace?
notes.back: Label the namespace pod-security.kubernetes.io/<mode>=<level>, e.g. pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted.
notes.extra: Modes: enforce rejects, audit logs to the audit log, warn returns a warning to the user.

notes.front: What does a pod/container securityContext control?
notes.back: Security settings such as runAsUser/runAsNonRoot, privileged, capabilities, readOnlyRootFilesystem, allowPrivilegeEscalation, and seccomp/AppArmor/SELinux profiles.

notes.front: What is the best-practice Linux capabilities setting in a securityContext?
notes.back: capabilities: {drop: ["ALL"], add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]}: drop everything, add back only what's needed. Never privileged or SYS_ADMIN.

notes.front: How do you apply the container runtime's default seccomp profile to a pod?
notes.back: securityContext.seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault (or Localhost with a profile file on the node). It blocks rarely needed, dangerous syscalls.

notes.front: How is an AppArmor profile applied to a container in current Kubernetes?
notes.back: securityContext.appArmorProfile (type RuntimeDefault or Localhost), GA in 1.30. Older clusters used the container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/<c> annotation.
notes.extra: A Localhost profile must already be loaded on the node.

notes.front: gVisor vs Kata Containers?
notes.back: gVisor: a user-space kernel intercepts the container's syscalls. Kata: each pod runs in a lightweight VM. Both sandbox untrusted or multi-tenant workloads beyond namespace isolation.
notes.analogy: gVisor is an interpreter who answers on the kernel's behalf; Kata gives each guest a house of their own.

notes.front: How does a pod select a sandboxed runtime such as gVisor?
notes.back: Set spec.runtimeClassName to a RuntimeClass, which maps to a CRI handler (e.g. runc, runsc, kata).

notes.front: How do you harden the kubelet API (port 10250), and why?
notes.back: --anonymous-auth=false, --authorization-mode=Webhook (not AlwaysAllow), and the NodeRestriction admission plugin. The kubelet can exec into pods and read logs, and NodeRestriction limits a node to its own objects.

notes.text: Kubernetes audit levels, least to most detail: {{c1::None}} → {{c2::Metadata}} (who, what, when) → {{c3::Request}} (+ request body) → {{c4::RequestResponse}} (+ response body).
notes.extra: Tip: log Secrets at Metadata only, or the audit log leaks them.

notes.front: Which kube-apiserver flags enable audit logging?
notes.back: --audit-policy-file (the rules) and --audit-log-path (log backend; a webhook backend is also possible).

notes.front: How do you enable encryption at rest for Secrets in etcd?
notes.back: Give kube-apiserver an EncryptionConfiguration via --encryption-provider-config, with a provider such as aescbc, aesgcm or KMS v2 first in the list.

notes.front: After enabling encryption at rest, why must existing Secrets be rewritten?
notes.back: Only new writes are encrypted. Existing Secrets stay unencrypted until rewritten: kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -.

notes.front: Why is etcd the most valuable asset to protect in a cluster?
notes.back: It holds all state, including Secrets (unencrypted by default): read access ≈ full cluster compromise. Protect it with mTLS, control-plane-only network access, encryption at rest and backups.

notes.text: Insecure Kubernetes defaults: all pod-to-pod traffic is {{c1::allowed (no NetworkPolicy)}}; ServiceAccount tokens are {{c2::auto-mounted}}; no {{c3::Pod Security}} level is enforced; Secrets are only {{c4::base64-encoded}} in etcd.

notes.front: In KCSA threat modelling, how is STRIDE applied to a cluster?
notes.back: Map each trust boundary (user→API server, API server→etcd, control plane→kubelet, pod→pod, cluster→cloud) to Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Info disclosure, DoS and Elevation of privilege, then choose controls.

notes.front: Why apply microsegmentation inside a cluster?
notes.back: Allowing only required pod-to-pod flows (NetworkPolicies or mesh authz) limits lateral movement after one pod is compromised.
notes.analogy: Watertight compartments in a ship: one breach floods a single compartment, not the whole hull.

notes.front: How do you minimize a container image's attack surface?
notes.back: Minimal/distroless base, multi-stage builds (no build tools), pin by digest, run as non-root, no embedded secrets, scan in CI. Fewer binaries → fewer CVEs and no shell for an attacker.

notes.front: What does Trivy scan for?
notes.back: Container images, filesystems and IaC: OS/library CVEs, misconfigurations and leaked secrets; it can also emit an SBOM. Usually run in CI to gate images before they reach the registry.

notes.front: What is kube-bench?
notes.back: A tool that checks a cluster against the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark (control-plane flags, file permissions, kubelet config) and reports pass/fail with remediation.

notes.front: Which supply-chain attack vectors does KCSA emphasize?
notes.back: Compromised base images, malicious or typosquatted dependencies, unsigned artifacts, leaked credentials, and tampered build systems.
notes.extra: Mitigations: SBOMs, image signing (Cosign), SLSA provenance, scanning, admission-time verification. Depth: Platform Engineering deck.

notes.front: What does Falco detect?
notes.back: Suspicious runtime behaviour from kernel syscall events (via eBPF), e.g. a shell spawned in a container, writes under /etc, sensitive file reads, unexpected connections.
notes.analogy: A CCTV camera inside the building, where admission control is the guard at the door.
notes.extra: Complements admission controls: it catches what happens after a pod is admitted.

notes.front: Tetragon vs Falco?
notes.back: Both are eBPF runtime security tools. Falco mainly detects and alerts on rules; Tetragon (Cilium project) can also enforce in-kernel, e.g. kill the offending process.

notes.front: Why does KCSA treat logging and monitoring as a security control?
notes.back: You can't respond to what you can't see. Audit logs, runtime detection (Falco) and metrics provide detection and forensics.

notes.front: What is the shared responsibility split in managed Kubernetes?
notes.back: The provider secures the control plane and infrastructure (the Cloud C); you secure workloads, RBAC, network policy, images and configs (Cluster/Container/Code).

notes.front: What is a kubeconfig context?
notes.back: A named tuple of cluster + user + namespace. The current context is the default target of every kubectl command.

notes.front: kubectl commands to switch context and to set the default namespace?
notes.back: kubectl config use-context <name>; kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=<ns>.

notes.front: How do you generate a manifest quickly in the exam instead of writing YAML by hand?
notes.back: --dry-run=client -o yaml, e.g. kubectl create deploy web --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > d.yaml.
notes.extra: Works with run, create job/cronjob/configmap/secret/role, expose.

notes.front: What is a static pod?
notes.back: A pod the kubelet runs directly from a manifest file on its node, without the scheduler. The API only shows a read-only mirror pod.

notes.front: Where does the kubelet look for static pod manifests on kubeadm clusters?
notes.back: The staticPodPath (--pod-manifest-path), default /etc/kubernetes/manifests.

notes.front: Why do kubeadm control-plane components run as static pods?
notes.back: The kubelet can start them before any API server exists, which solves the bootstrap chicken-and-egg problem.

notes.front: Which flags does etcdctl snapshot save need on a kubeadm cluster?
notes.back: --endpoints, --cacert, --cert, --key (etcd CA and client cert, from the etcd manifest), with ETCDCTL_API=3.

notes.front: How do you restore an etcd snapshot on a kubeadm cluster?
notes.back: etcdctl snapshot restore snap.db --data-dir /var/lib/etcd-new (newer: etcdutl), then point the etcd static pod's data hostPath at the new directory.

notes.text: kubeadm upgrade on the control-plane node: upgrade the {{c1::kubeadm}} package → run {{c2::kubeadm upgrade plan, then kubeadm upgrade apply vX.Y.Z}} → drain, upgrade {{c3::kubelet and kubectl}}, restart kubelet, uncordon.

notes.front: kubeadm upgrade: what do you do on each worker node?
notes.back: Upgrade kubeadm, run kubeadm upgrade node, drain, upgrade kubelet + kubectl, restart kubelet, uncordon.

notes.front: How many minor versions can a kubeadm upgrade skip?
notes.back: None: upgrade one minor version at a time (e.g. 1.30 → 1.31 → 1.32).

notes.front: kubectl cordon vs drain?
notes.back: cordon: mark the node unschedulable only. drain: cordon + evict its pods, respecting PodDisruptionBudgets. uncordon re-enables scheduling.
notes.extra: Typical flags: --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data.

notes.front: How long are kubeadm certificates valid, and how do you check and renew them?
notes.back: Leaf certs 1 year, CA 10 years. kubeadm certs check-expiration; kubeadm certs renew all. kubeadm upgrade also renews them.

notes.front: A pod is stuck in Pending. First triage step, and the usual causes?
notes.back: kubectl describe pod → Events. Causes: not enough CPU/memory, unmet nodeSelector/affinity/taints, unbound PVC, or no Ready nodes.

notes.front: A pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. How do you see why its last run died?
notes.back: kubectl logs <pod> --previous for the crashed instance's logs, and kubectl describe pod for the exit code and reason (e.g. OOMKilled).

notes.front: The API server is down on a kubeadm cluster. Where do you look?
notes.back: kubectl won't work, so on the node: journalctl -u kubelet, crictl ps -a / crictl logs, and /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml (bad flags, certs, etcd reachability).

notes.text: The three pillars of observability: {{c1::metrics}} (aggregatable numeric time series), {{c2::logs}} (discrete timestamped events), {{c3::traces}} (one request's path across services).

notes.front: What does kubectl top need, and what doesn't it give you?
notes.back: The metrics-server add-on (metrics.k8s.io API). It shows live node/pod CPU and memory only, with no history; use Prometheus for that.

notes.front: node_exporter vs kube-state-metrics vs metrics-server?
notes.back: node_exporter: host CPU/memory/disk. kube-state-metrics: object state (desired replicas, pod phase). metrics-server: live usage for kubectl top and HPA, not for Prometheus.

notes.text: Prometheus metric types: a {{c1::Counter}} only goes up (resets on restart); a {{c2::Gauge}} goes up and down; a {{c3::Histogram}} counts observations into buckets (+ _sum/_count); a {{c4::Summary}} computes quantiles client-side.

notes.front: Histogram vs Summary: why prefer histograms in Prometheus?
notes.back: Histogram buckets can be aggregated across instances and quantiles computed at query time. Summary quantiles are per instance and can't be meaningfully averaged.

notes.front: How does Prometheus collect metrics?
notes.back: It pulls: it scrapes each target's HTTP /metrics endpoint on an interval. Pull makes target health visible (up) and keeps config central.
notes.analogy: A meter reader walking the route, rather than every household posting in its own readings.

notes.front: What is the Prometheus Pushgateway for, and what's its caveat?
notes.back: Short-lived batch jobs push metrics to it and Prometheus scrapes it. Caveat: pushed metrics persist until deleted (stale values) and it isn't for long-running services.

notes.front: What uniquely identifies a Prometheus time series?
notes.back: The metric name plus the full set of label key/value pairs.

notes.front: Why is a user ID a bad Prometheus label?
notes.back: Each distinct label value creates a new series. Unbounded cardinality explodes memory and query cost.

notes.front: PromQL: instant vector vs range vector?
notes.back: Instant vector: one sample per series at a single timestamp. Range vector: samples over a window (metric[5m]). rate() takes a range vector and returns an instant vector.

notes.front: PromQL rate() vs irate()?
notes.back: rate(): per-second average over the whole window; smooth, use for alerts and dashboards. irate(): uses only the last two samples; spiky, fast-reacting.

notes.front: Why always wrap counters in rate()/increase() instead of subtracting raw values?
notes.back: Counters reset to 0 when a process restarts. rate()/increase() detect and correct for resets; manual differences go negative or wrong.

notes.front: PromQL for p95 latency from a histogram?
notes.back: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))
notes.extra: _bucket series are cumulative, labelled by le (upper bound). Keep le in the sum by.

notes.front: What is a Prometheus exporter?
notes.back: A process that exposes metrics, in Prometheus text format, for a system that doesn't do so natively, e.g. node_exporter (host), blackbox_exporter (probes).

notes.front: Why does Prometheus need service discovery in Kubernetes?
notes.back: Targets come and go, so kubernetes_sd_configs discovers pods/services/nodes dynamically, and relabeling decides which to scrape and which labels they get.

notes.front: What does a Prometheus scrape_config define?
notes.back: A job_name, interval/timeout, metrics path and scheme, target discovery (static_configs or *_sd_configs) and relabel_configs. Each series gets a job label.

notes.front: What is a Prometheus recording rule, and why use one?
notes.back: A precomputed expression saved as a new series at each evaluation (record:). It speeds up expensive dashboard queries and stabilizes alert expressions.

notes.front: What does the for: clause in a Prometheus alerting rule do?
notes.back: The condition must hold continuously for that duration before the alert moves from pending to firing, which cuts flapping.

notes.text: Alertmanager: {{c1::grouping}} batches related alerts into one notification; {{c2::inhibition}} suppresses alerts while a higher-level alert fires; {{c3::silencing}} mutes matching alerts for a time window.

notes.front: Prometheus storage: what's local, and how do you get long-term retention / HA?
notes.back: A local single-node TSDB (in-memory head block + WAL, compacted to disk blocks). For long-term retention and HA, remote_write to Thanos, Mimir or Cortex.

notes.text: Metric selection methods: {{c1::USE}} for resources (Utilization, Saturation, Errors); {{c2::RED}} for request-driven services (Rate, Errors, Duration).

notes.front: What is OpenTelemetry?
notes.back: The CNCF vendor-neutral standard (API, SDKs, Collector, OTLP) for generating, collecting and exporting traces, metrics and logs.
notes.extra: Also emerging: profiles; plus baggage for propagating key/values.

notes.front: OpenTelemetry: span vs trace?
notes.back: A span is one timed operation (name, start/end, attributes, status). A trace is the tree of spans sharing a trace ID: one request's path across services.
notes.analogy: A trace is a parcel's tracking history; each span is one scan at a depot.

notes.front: What is context propagation in OpenTelemetry?
notes.back: Passing trace context (trace ID, span ID, flags) across service boundaries, usually in the W3C traceparent/tracestate headers, so spans join one trace.

notes.text: OpenTelemetry Collector pipeline: {{c1::receivers}} (ingest, e.g. OTLP) → {{c2::processors}} (batch, filter, transform) → {{c3::exporters}} (send to backends).
notes.extra: Decouples apps from observability backends: switch vendors by changing Collector config.

notes.front: Why deploy the OTel Collector as both agent and gateway?
notes.back: Agent (per node/sidecar): local, low-latency collection. Gateway (central pool): heavy processing (tail sampling, batching) and fan-out to backends.

notes.front: What is OTLP?
notes.back: The OpenTelemetry Protocol: the native wire format (protobuf over gRPC or HTTP) for traces, metrics and logs between SDKs, Collectors and backends.

notes.front: OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation vs manual instrumentation?
notes.back: Auto: agents/libraries instrument common frameworks with no code changes. Manual: you call the API for custom spans/metrics around business logic. Usually combine both.

notes.front: OpenTelemetry API vs SDK?
notes.back: The API is the interface code instruments against (a no-op if unconfigured). The SDK implements sampling, processing and export. Libraries depend only on the API; the app wires in the SDK.

notes.front: Why do OpenTelemetry semantic conventions matter?
notes.back: Standard attribute/metric names (service.name, http.request.method) make telemetry consistent across languages and vendors, so dashboards and queries are reusable.

notes.front: What is a Resource in OpenTelemetry?
notes.back: Immutable attributes describing the telemetry source (service.name, version, host, k8s pod), attached to all its signals.

notes.front: Head sampling vs tail sampling?
notes.back: Head: decided at trace start; cheap but blind to the outcome. Tail: decided after the whole trace is seen (keep errors/slow traces); done in the Collector, needs buffering.

notes.front: What is an exemplar?
notes.back: A sample on a metric (e.g. in a histogram bucket) carrying a trace ID, linking an aggregate back to a representative trace for drill-down.

notes.front: OpenTelemetry span kinds: which pair describes a synchronous call, and which an async message?
notes.back: Sync: CLIENT (caller) → SERVER (callee). Async: PRODUCER → CONSUMER. In-process work is INTERNAL.
notes.extra: Span status values: Unset, Ok, Error.

notes.text: OpenTelemetry was formed by merging {{c1::OpenTracing}} (tracing API) and {{c2::OpenCensus}} (metrics + tracing libraries).

notes.front: What is a service mesh?
notes.back: An infrastructure layer (proxies + control plane) that handles service-to-service traffic management, mTLS and telemetry transparently, moving those concerns out of app code.
notes.analogy: Each service gets a personal assistant who places and answers its calls, encrypting, retrying and logging them, so the service just talks.

notes.front: Istio control plane vs data plane?
notes.back: Control plane: istiod (discovery, config, certificate authority), pushing config via xDS. Data plane: Envoy sidecars per pod, or ztunnel + waypoint proxies in ambient mode.

notes.front: Istio sidecar mode vs ambient mode?
notes.back: Sidecar: an Envoy in every pod (full L7, per-pod overhead). Ambient: no sidecars; a per-node ztunnel does L4 mTLS, and optional waypoint proxies add L7 only where needed.

notes.front: What is ztunnel in Istio ambient mode?
notes.back: A per-node proxy (DaemonSet, written in Rust) handling L4 mTLS, authentication and telemetry for all pods on the node.

notes.front: What is HBONE in Istio ambient mode?
notes.back: HTTP-Based Overlay Network Environment: mTLS-encrypted HTTP CONNECT tunnelling (port 15008) carrying traffic between ztunnels and waypoints.

notes.front: What is an Istio waypoint proxy, and how is it deployed?
notes.back: An Envoy providing L7 features (routing, retries, L7 authz) in ambient mode, shared per namespace/service account. Deployed as a Gateway API Gateway with gatewayClassName: istio-waypoint.

notes.front: What does an Istio VirtualService configure?
notes.back: L7 routing rules for a host: match on URI/headers, then route by weight to destinations/subsets, with retries, timeouts and fault injection.

notes.front: Istio VirtualService vs DestinationRule?
notes.back: VirtualService = how requests are routed to a host. DestinationRule = what applies after routing: named subsets (v1/v2 by pod labels), LB policy, connection pools, outlier detection.

notes.front: How do you run a weighted canary in Istio?
notes.back: In a VirtualService, split route weights across subsets (e.g. 90% v1, 10% v2) defined in a DestinationRule, then shift the weights gradually.

notes.front: What does an Istio Gateway resource do?
notes.back: Configures a load balancer at the mesh edge: which ports, protocols and hosts are exposed. A VirtualService bound to the Gateway routes that traffic to services.

notes.front: What does an Istio ServiceEntry do?
notes.back: Adds an external service to the mesh registry, so traffic to it gets Istio routing, policy, mTLS origination and telemetry.

notes.text: Istio PeerAuthentication mTLS modes: {{c1::STRICT}} accepts mTLS only; {{c2::PERMISSIVE}} accepts mTLS or plaintext (the default, eases migration); {{c3::DISABLE}} turns mTLS off.

notes.front: Istio RequestAuthentication vs AuthorizationPolicy?
notes.back: RequestAuthentication validates end-user JWTs (issuer/JWKS); it authenticates but doesn't authorize. AuthorizationPolicy ALLOWs/DENYs by identity, namespace, JWT claims, method, path.

notes.front: How does Istio give each workload an mTLS identity?
notes.back: istiod acts as a CA issuing X.509 certs with a SPIFFE ID derived from the pod's ServiceAccount: spiffe://<trust-domain>/ns/<ns>/sa/<sa>.

notes.front: What is Istio fault injection for?
notes.back: Deliberately injecting delays or aborts (e.g. HTTP 500 for 10% of requests) via a VirtualService to test resilience without changing app code.

notes.front: What is outlier detection in Istio?
notes.back: A DestinationRule setting that ejects endpoints returning consecutive errors from the LB pool for a cooldown, so one bad instance doesn't drag the service down (circuit breaking).
notes.analogy: A relay team benching a runner who keeps dropping the baton, then letting them back after a rest.

notes.front: istioctl analyze vs istioctl proxy-config?
notes.back: analyze: validates mesh config for problems. proxy-config <cluster|route|listener|endpoint> <pod>: dumps the Envoy config a proxy actually received, the main tool for routing bugs.

notes.front: What telemetry does Istio give you without app changes?
notes.back: Proxies emit standard L7 metrics (request count, duration, size), access logs, trace spans and service-graph data, feeding Prometheus, Grafana, Jaeger and Kiali.

notes.front: Why does Cilium use eBPF instead of iptables?
notes.back: eBPF programs run in-kernel at hooks (tc, XDP, sockets), so policy, Service load balancing and visibility use efficient hash-map lookups instead of long linear iptables chains.
notes.extra: eBPF internals: see the Linux deck.

notes.front: How does Cilium's identity-based policy differ from IP-based rules?
notes.back: Each endpoint (usually a pod) gets a numeric security identity derived from its labels; policy is enforced on identities, so it stays correct as pods churn and IPs are reused.
notes.analogy: Checking ID badges instead of desk numbers: people can move desks without the security rules breaking.
notes.extra: Inspect with cilium endpoint list.

notes.front: What does a CiliumNetworkPolicy add over a standard NetworkPolicy?
notes.back: Standard policy is L3/L4 only. CiliumNetworkPolicy adds L7 rules (e.g. allow only GET /api, Kafka topics), DNS-based egress, and cluster-wide policies.

notes.front: How does Cilium allow egress to an external service by DNS name?
notes.back: toFQDNs rules: Cilium intercepts DNS answers, learns the resolved IPs and allows egress only to them, so you don't need to know external IPs in advance.

notes.front: What is Hubble?
notes.back: Cilium's eBPF-based observability layer: flow visibility (who talked to whom, allowed/denied, L7 verbs), a service map and metrics, without app instrumentation. CLI: hubble observe.

notes.front: What does kube-proxy replacement mean in Cilium?
notes.back: Cilium implements Service load balancing (ClusterIP, NodePort, …) directly in eBPF, so kube-proxy and its iptables rules aren't needed; it scales better with many Services.

notes.front: Cilium agent vs Cilium operator?
notes.back: Agent (DaemonSet): per node, manages eBPF programs/maps, identities, policy and Service LB. Operator: cluster-wide tasks such as IPAM and garbage collection.

notes.front: What is Cilium Cluster Mesh?
notes.back: Connects multiple clusters into one network and identity domain: cross-cluster service discovery, global services with failover, and network policy across clusters.

notes.front: What transparent encryption options does Cilium offer?
notes.back: WireGuard (simple, fast) or IPsec, enabled at the agent level to encrypt node-to-node pod traffic with no app changes.

notes.front: How does Cilium relate to Ingress and the Gateway API?
notes.back: Cilium can be the Ingress / Gateway API controller itself (Envoy + eBPF), consolidating CNI, load balancing and ingress in one dataplane.

notes.front: What is cloud native, in essence (CNCF definition)?
notes.back: Building and running scalable apps in dynamic environments with containers, microservices, immutable infrastructure and declarative APIs, giving loosely coupled, resilient, observable systems that change often with low risk.

notes.text: CNCF project maturity levels: {{c1::Sandbox}} (early) → {{c2::Incubating}} (growing adoption) → {{c3::Graduated}} (mature, e.g. Kubernetes, Prometheus, Envoy).
The Open Container Initiative (OCI) defines the {{c1::image-spec}} (image format), the {{c2::runtime-spec}} (how to run a filesystem bundle) and the {{c3::distribution-spec}} (registry API).
notes.extra: Why it matters: an image built by any tool runs on any compliant runtime and registry.

notes.front: What is the gist of the Twelve-Factor App?
notes.back: Principles for portable cloud apps, e.g. config in the environment, stateless disposable processes, backing services as attached resources, build/release/run separation, logs as event streams.

notes.front: What is serverless, and what does Knative bring to Kubernetes?
notes.back: Running code without managing servers, scaling to zero when idle. Knative adds this to Kubernetes.

notes.text: Knative components: {{c1::Serving}} provides request-driven autoscaling including scale-to-zero; {{c2::Eventing}} provides event sources, brokers and delivery.

notes.front: Kustomize vs Helm?
notes.back: Kustomize: template-free; a base plus per-environment overlays of plain YAML patches, built into kubectl (kubectl apply -k). Helm: Go templates + packaging, versioned releases and rollback.
notes.extra: Helm depth: Platform Engineering deck.

notes.front: What is GitOps (KCNA-level definition)?
notes.back: An operating model where Git is the single source of truth for declarative infra/app state and an in-cluster agent continuously reconciles the cluster to it.
notes.extra: Principles, Argo CD and Flux depth: Platform Engineering deck.

notes.front: How does GitOps relate to CI/CD?
notes.back: CI builds and tests artifacts outside the cluster. GitOps is one way to do the CD half: declarative, Git-driven, pull-based and continuously reconciled.

notes.front: Why separate the app source repo from the config (deployment) repo in GitOps?
notes.back: CI builds the code and just bumps an image tag in the config repo; the GitOps agent deploys from the config repo. Deploy state stays declarative, auditable and decoupled from builds.

notes.front: What is a sound promotion strategy across environments?
notes.back: Promote the same immutable artifact (image digest) dev → staging → prod via Git changes, gated by automated tests/policy and progressive delivery. Kargo can orchestrate it.

notes.front: Canary vs blue-green deployment?
notes.back: Canary: shift a small % of traffic to the new version, watch metrics, ramp up. Blue-green: a full standby environment, then switch all traffic at once (instant rollback).
notes.analogy: Canary: let a few diners taste the new recipe first. Blue-green: cook a full second kitchen, then swap which one serves the room.

notes.front: Argo CD vs Argo Rollouts: who does progressive delivery?
notes.back: Argo CD only syncs manifests. Argo Rollouts' Rollout CRD runs canary/blue-green steps; Argo CD deploys the Rollout object.

notes.front: What is an Argo Rollouts AnalysisTemplate?
notes.back: Metric queries (e.g. Prometheus) with success/failure conditions evaluated during rollout steps. A breach automatically aborts and rolls back the release.

notes.front: What is Argo Workflows?
notes.back: A Kubernetes-native workflow engine (Workflow CRD) where each step runs in a container, ordered as steps or a DAG. Used for CI, batch/data and ML pipelines.

notes.front: Argo Workflows: steps vs dag templates?
notes.back: steps: sequential stages (items within a stage run in parallel). dag: tasks declare dependencies and run as soon as those finish, for more flexible parallelism.

notes.front: What is Argo Events?
notes.back: Event-driven automation: EventSources ingest events (webhooks, queues, cron) and Sensors evaluate dependencies and trigger actions, e.g. start an Argo Workflow.

notes.front: Kyverno Policy vs ClusterPolicy?
notes.back: Policy is namespaced and applies only in its namespace; ClusterPolicy applies cluster-wide. Both hold rules with match/exclude selectors.

notes.front: What does a Kyverno policy's failure action (Enforce vs Audit) control?
notes.back: Enforce: a failed validate rule blocks the request. Audit: allowed but recorded in a PolicyReport. Roll out in Audit first, then switch to Enforce.

notes.front: What are Kyverno PolicyReports?
notes.back: Custom resources holding per-resource results (pass, fail, warn, error, skip) reflecting current state, not history. PolicyReport is namespaced; ClusterPolicyReport is cluster-wide.

notes.front: Typical use case for a Kyverno generate rule?
notes.back: When a Namespace is created, automatically create a default-deny NetworkPolicy and a ResourceQuota in it, optionally kept in sync with their source.

notes.front: What is a Kyverno PolicyException?
notes.back: A resource exempting specific resources/namespaces from named policy rules: a scoped, governed escape hatch instead of weakening the policy itself.

notes.front: How do you test Kyverno policies before they reach a cluster?
notes.back: Kyverno CLI: kyverno apply runs policies against manifests locally; kyverno test runs declarative test cases. Both fit in CI.

notes.front: Platform engineering vs DevOps?
notes.back: DevOps is a culture of shared ownership between dev and ops. Platform engineering builds an Internal Developer Platform as a product, giving teams self-service paved roads so each team doesn't reinvent infrastructure.
notes.extra: Depth (golden paths, Backstage, TVP): Platform Engineering deck.

notes.front: What is the CNCF Platform Engineering Maturity Model for?
notes.back: Assessing a platform across aspects (investment, adoption, interfaces, operations, measurement) at levels Provisional → Operational → Scalable → Optimizing, to plan its evolution.

notes.front: Continuous Integration vs Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment?
notes.back: CI: merge, build and test often. Continuous Delivery: every passing build is releasable; prod deploy is a manual click. Continuous Deployment: every passing build goes to prod automatically.

notes.front: What does chmod 750 file grant?
notes.back: Owner rwx (7), group r-x (5), others nothing (0); r=4, w=2, x=1.
notes.extra: Symbolic form: chmod u+x f; ownership: chown user:group f.

notes.text: Special permission bits: {{c1::SUID}} (4xxx) runs an executable as its owner; {{c2::SGID}} (2xxx) runs as the group / new files inherit the directory's group; the {{c3::sticky bit}} (1xxx) on a directory lets only owners delete their files (e.g. /tmp).

notes.front: With umask 022, what permissions do new files and directories get?
notes.back: Files 644, directories 755 (base 666/777 minus the mask; files never get execute by default).

notes.front: systemctl start vs enable?
notes.back: start runs the unit now; enable makes it start at boot (enable --now does both). After editing unit files: systemctl daemon-reload.

notes.front: What replaced SysV runlevels in systemd, and how do you set the default?
notes.back: Targets: multi-user.target (≈ runlevel 3) and graphical.target (≈ 5). systemctl set-default <target>; switch now with systemctl isolate.

notes.front: journalctl: a unit's logs, follow mode, current boot only?
notes.back: journalctl -u <unit>, -f to follow, -b for this boot. Also --since "10 min ago", -p err.
notes.extra: Persistent logs need /var/log/journal to exist. Key for kubelet debugging: journalctl -u kubelet.

notes.front: Modern commands for IP addresses, routes and listening sockets?
notes.back: ip addr, ip route, ip link set dev eth0 up (iproute2); ss -tulpn for listening sockets (replaces netstat).

notes.text: LVM layers: {{c1::Physical Volumes}} (disks/partitions) are pooled into a {{c2::Volume Group}}, which is carved into {{c3::Logical Volumes}} that you format and mount.
notes.extra: Grow: lvextend then resize2fs / xfs_growfs (or lvextend -r).

notes.front: How do you make a mount persistent across reboots safely?
notes.back: Add an /etc/fstab line (UUID=… /mnt/data xfs defaults 0 0), using UUIDs from blkid, and test with mount -a before rebooting.

notes.front: df vs du?
notes.back: df -h: free/used space per filesystem. du -sh <dir>: space used by a directory tree.
notes.extra: lsblk lists block devices.

notes.front: kill vs kill -9?
notes.back: kill sends SIGTERM (15): the process can clean up. kill -9 sends SIGKILL: immediate and uncatchable; last resort.
notes.extra: Same model as pod termination: SIGTERM, grace period, then SIGKILL. Find PIDs with pgrep -f.

notes.text: Cron fields, in order: {{c1::minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week}}. 0 2 * * 1 means {{c2::02:00 every Monday}}.
notes.extra: Same syntax as a Kubernetes CronJob schedule.

notes.front: Package management: Debian family vs RHEL family?
notes.back: Debian/Ubuntu: apt / dpkg with .deb. RHEL/Fedora: dnf (yum) / rpm with .rpm.

notes.front: SELinux enforcing vs permissive mode?
notes.back: Enforcing: denials are blocked and logged. Permissive: only logged, for debugging. Check/toggle with getenforce / setenforce 0|1; persist in /etc/selinux/config.

notes.front: Why is usermod -G dangerous without -a?
notes.back: -G alone replaces the user's supplementary groups; -aG appends.
notes.extra: Create a user with home dir: useradd -m -s /bin/bash alice, then passwd alice.

notes.front: What does cmd > out.log 2>&1 do?
notes.back: Sends stdout to out.log, then points stderr at the same place, so both go to the file. Order matters: 2>&1 > f leaves stderr on the terminal.

notes.text: Text tools: {{c1::grep}} searches lines by pattern; {{c2::sed}} stream-edits (s/old/new/g); {{c3::awk}} processes fields ('{print $2}').

notes.front: How do you set up passwordless SSH key authentication?
notes.back: ssh-keygen, then ssh-copy-id user@host (appends the public key to the server's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys). Keep the private key at 600 permissions.

notes.front: Hard link vs symbolic link?
notes.back: Hard link: another name for the same inode; can't cross filesystems or link directories. Symlink: a pointer to a path; can cross filesystems and can dangle.
notes.analogy: A hard link is a second name on the same house deed; a symlink is a signpost pointing to an address, which may have been demolished.

notes.front: Allow HTTP through firewalld vs ufw?
notes.back: firewalld: firewall-cmd --add-service=http --permanent then --reload. ufw: ufw allow 80/tcp, ufw enable. Both front nftables/iptables.

notes.front: tar commands to create, list and extract a gzip archive?
notes.back: Create tar -czf out.tar.gz dir/; list tar -tzf out.tar.gz; extract tar -xzf out.tar.gz (c/t/x = create/list/extract, z = gzip, f = file).
